findings.title: Sae placebo pct count mismatch (Results, Safety, paragraph 2; Table 2, All SAEs row)
findings.description: 8.82% is a perfectly achievable share of 68 -- GRIM passes -- but the count it recovers is 6, while the sentence and Table 2 both state 7 placebo patients with an SAE. 7/68 is 10.29%. So the percentage and its own count contradict each other by one patient. This is not a GRIM failure; it is the tool's recovered `rounded_count` disagreeing with the printed count, which is why it is graded suspicious rather than impossible. The most economical explanation is that the placebo DEATH percentage (6/68) was carried into the SAE sentence, which would also explain the neighbouring 8.83% error.

findings.title: Cerebrolysin arm disposition shortfall (Results, Patient disposition)
findings.description: Both failing sums are the same two patients seen twice. The placebo arm reconciles EXACTLY (52 + 6 + 1 + 9 = 68), which localises the discrepancy entirely to the Cerebrolysin arm: 78 randomised minus 67 completers is 11 discontinuations, but only 9 are enumerated (6 deaths + 3 consent withdrawn). The enumerated reasons do sum correctly to the '25 cases' the paper claims -- the internal arithmetic of that sentence is sound -- so the error is that 25 is itself two short of the 27 the completer counts require. 21 of the 23 sums checked reconcile exactly, including every Table 1 count and percentage column and every Table 2 column.

findings.title: Itt locf vs day90 n contradiction
findings.description: The paper declares ITT with LOCF, and the Fig. 2 caption duly reports n=146 for the SST analysis. But the loss of significance for the CNS A1 subscore at day 90 is explained by attrition to 119 patients -- which cannot happen under LOCF, where the day-21 value is carried forward for the 27 non-completers. Either the day-90 analysis was in fact a completers-only analysis (contradicting the declared method), or the stated explanation for the null day-90 result is wrong. Recorded as a design/reporting inconsistency under rulebook rule 5; no arithmetic is violated.

consequence.explanation: The paper's explanation for why its neurological-outcome benefit disappeared at day 90 -- reduced sample size -- is unavailable under the analysis method it says it used.

findings.title: Conmed cerebrolysin no shared denominator
findings.description: No n in [2, 78] lets all five percentages pass GRIM under round-half; the paper's own arm size of 78 is not viable (11% requires n in a set that excludes 78 -- 8/78 rounds to 10 and 9/78 to 12). The tool found n=76 viable under the TRUNCATION convention, which SPSS and several journals use, and correctly capped the verdict at suspicious rather than impossible for exactly that reason. At whole-percentage precision this check has little power and the finding is weak on its own; it is recorded because it concerns the same arm whose disposition is two patients short and whose AE rate is GRIM-impossible, not because whole-number percentages are individually alarming.

findings.title: Subgroup p smaller than full sample (Results, Efficacy, paragraph 3)
findings.description: For both cognitive instruments the right-hemisphere subgroup (37 + 37 = 74 patients) yields a p-value at least two orders of magnitude smaller than the full sample of 146 -- and for the MMSE the full sample is null while half of it reaches p<0.001. That pattern requires the left-hemisphere subgroup to be null or reversed, which is what the authors argue (aphasia in left-hemisphere stroke). The argument is clinically reasonable and the subgroups WERE pre-specified in the Methods, which counts in the paper's favour. What is missing is any interaction test, any subgroup effect estimate, and any exact p; the claim is therefore not checkable. Recorded as a design observation under rulebook rule 5

anchors.quote: The drug=placebo difference was most pronounced in the sub-group of patients with a stroke in the right brain hemisphere (p<0.001; Mantel-Haenszel test). The difference in the MMSE score did not reach statistical significance, however, a highly significant effect of Cerebrolysin versus placebo was observed for the right-sided stroke subgroup (p<0.001, Mantel-Haenszel test) for this instrument.

These (0.59, 0.40, 0.35) are unremarkable and spread across the middle of the range, which is what honest randomisation looks like. Three rows is far too few to support any omnibus similarity test in any case.

The range/2 bound the tool uses ignores the mean, and the tighter mean-conditional bound is what would settle whether that SD is attainable. No available tool computes it, so this is recorded as unresolved rather than estimated by hand. Tolerances here are degraded: the `decimals` argument crashes this MCP wrapper (same string-coercion defect as grim_check), so the checks ran with a flat 1% margin instead of the printed precision.

findings.title: Nonstandard alpha threshold (Results, paragraph following Table 2)
findings.description: The Methods declare a single criterion, p<0.05. Every other result in the paper is reported against a conventional bound (0.05, 0.01, 0.001, or 0.1 for trends). This one result is reported against 0.015, a threshold that appears nowhere else and corresponds to no standard convention. A bound of that shape is what you get by rounding an exact p upward to the next tidy value (an exact p of, say, 0.014 reported as '<0.015'), which if so means an exact p was available and not printed. This cannot be resolved: with no test statistic and no CGI summary data, stalt_check has nothing to work from. Recorded as a reporting irregularity, not an arithmetic anomaly.
